en: Oṃ! Homage to Vajravārāhī;
homage be to Vajrayoginī, whose very nature is emptiness and compassion.
He who manifests the diversity of forms through the various distinctions of worldly existence.
She who, by virtue of the nectar-forest of the nectar of perfect enlightenment, is illuminated by clarity;
she who, being peaceful, spreads a redness beyond passion among the people to be trained;
and she who bears a vajra, a stainless skull-cup, and a khaṭvāṅga staff, possessing fierce splendor.
May this Blessed Lady Vajravilāsinī be for your prosperity.

In this context, a yogi who possesses undivided faith in the Guru and the Buddha, who has properly grasped the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), who has correctly received initiation, whose mass of hair is loosened, and whose mouth is purified by the application of the five powders (*pañcavaṭikā*) and so forth, sits upon a comfortable seat in a certain place such as a charnel ground or a mountain—or seated directly upon a corpse—reciting: *oṃ a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ e ai o au aṃ aḥ ka kha ga gha ṅa ca cha ja jha ña ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa ta tha da dha na pa pha ba bha ma ya ra la va śa ṣa*.

Having uttered three times "sa ha kṣa huṃ huṃ phaṭ"—which consists of the rows of vowels and consonants radiating five-colored rays—one should visualize [the mantra] standing encircling [the deity], with the multitude of deities of the three wheels radiating and crushing the host of obstructing spirits. This is the purification of speech.

One should resolve upon the purity of the aggregates and so forth, for acts such as worship arising from the purity of the aggregates and so forth become a swift cause for enlightenment. In that regard, Vairocana and the others are to be determined as being like foam, bubbles, a mirage, a plantain tree, and an illusion within the [five aggregates] beginning with form and ending with consciousness; likewise, Akṣobhya is [to be determined] in this way. Alternatively, their very purity is the resolve (*adhimokṣa*) upon the deities Vairocana and the rest. One should summon the heroes and yoginīs residing in the world-systems of the ten directions. [End of edition page].

Oṃ! All phenomena are pure through yoga; I am pure through yoga. Oṃ āḥ aralli hoḥ jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ! Vajra-ḍākinī, you are the *samaya*; behold! At midnight, one should offer the *bali* with the *vajrāñjali* mudrā and the upward-flourishing (*ūrdhvavikaca*) mudrā. *Hoḥ!* [126]

Oṃ kha kha khāhi khāhi! May all yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, unmādas, apasmāras, ḍākas, ḍākinīs, and so forth, accept this bali offering; may they protect the samaya; for the purpose of eating, drinking, and smelling, do not transgress, but become my companions for the sake of increasing all happiness through omniscience! Huṃ huṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā! This is the purification of the bali mantra.

In that regard, within form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, there are Vairocana, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, Amoghasiddhi, and Vajrasattva. Within the suchness (*tathatā*) of form and the other aggregates, there is Akṣobhya. These six should be understood by their colors as white, yellow, red, green, white, and black. Vairocana has his right hand raised holding a wheel, and his left hand at his hip holding a bell together with a lotus.

Ratnasaṃbhava, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi hold a jewel, a red lotus, and a crossed-vajra respectively in their right hands, which are held playfully; their left hands hold bells at the waist. Vajrasattva and Vajradhara have their right hands held playfully at the heart, while their left hands hold bells at the waist with the palms joined. Akṣobhya-Vajra has his right hand in the earth-touching mudrā accompanied by a vajra, while his left hand holds a bell at the waist with the palms joined.

In the eyes, ears, nose, mouth, and tactile sense, there are Mohavajra, Dveṣavajra, Īrṣyāvajra, Rāgavajra, and Mātsaryavajra; their internal names are Kṣitigarbha, Vajrapāṇi, Khagarbha, Lokeśvara, and Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin; they are white, black, yellow, red, and dark green in color respectively. In all the sense-bases (āyatana), there is Aiśvaryavajra, whose internal name is Samantabhadra, and he is white. Mohavajra has his right hand raised in the gesture of striking with a mace, and his left hand gracefully holds a bell at his heart.

Dveṣavajra has his right hand at his heart holding a vajra, and his left hand at his hip holding a bell with its interior facing outward. Īrṣyāvajra, Rāgavajra, and Mātsaryavajra have their right arms raised playfully, holding respectively a jewel, a red lotus, and a crossed-vajra; their left hands hold bells at their hearts in a playful manner. Aiśvaryavajra, however, has his right hand at his heart holding a vajra, and his left hand at his hip holding a bell with its interior facing outward. Therein... [ed. p.]

He is Mohavajra because he destroys delusion; he is Dveṣavajra because he hates hatred; and there are the three beginning with Īrṣyāvajra because they destroy envy, all attachment, and avarice. He is Aiśvaryavajra because he bestows all sovereignty; these have as their intrinsic nature the purification of the elements of earth, water, fire, and air.

Pātinī, Maraṇī, Ākarṣaṇī, and Narteśvarī are yellow, black, red, and green in color respectively; they each have one face and four arms. Their two right hands hold a discus-sword, a vajra-sword, a lotus-sword, and a sword, while their two left hands hold a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga. They are named Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍarā, and Tārā, and their intrinsic nature is that of the space-element (ākāśadhātu).

Padmajālinī is smoke-colored, with three faces—smoke, white, and red—and six arms. Her three left hands hold a skull-cup (*kapāla*), a khaṭvāṅga staff, and a noose; her three right hands are adorned with a hook (*aṅkuśa*), a Brahmā-head, and a flaying-knife (*kartī*). She has the nature of the Vajra-Dharmadhātu. In that regard, Pātanyā and the others accomplish their activities according to their names. Vairocana and the others stand in the *ālīḍha* posture, wear crowns of matted hair, have three eyes, and are adorned with the five mudrās. The goddesses have loose hair, are naked, stand in the *ālīḍha* posture, have three eyes, and possess the five mudrās.

Then, having visualized within the hollow of one's own heart a red syllable *vaṃ* situated upon a solar disc produced from the seed-syllable *raṃ*, and having removed internal impurities by means of its rays emerging from every pore of the skin, one should attract and bring before oneself the previously described mandala-circle of the Bhagavatī, as well as the Gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas; having visualized them in the sky in front and paid homage, one should worship them with the sixteen goddesses, such as Vīṇā and the others, who have been projected from the rays of the seed-syllable.

Therein, the Vīṇā, Vaṃśā, Mṛdaṅgā, and Murajā have one face and four arms; they are blue, yellow, red, and green respectively, intent upon playing their respective instruments with their two principal hands, while their other two hands hold a vajra and a vajra-bell. Hāsyā, Lāsyā, Gītā, and Nṛtyā have one face and four arms; they are reddish, blue, yellow, and green respectively. Hāsyā has her two principal hands engaged in the gesture of laughter. Lāsyā has her two principal hands engaged in the gesture of dance, holding a vajra and a vajra-bell within them.

Gītā has two principal arms holding a bell-metal gong (kaṃsīkā); Nṛtyā has two principal arms performing the gestures of a lotus. In the other right and left arms of these [deities], there are a skull-cup (kapāla) and a khaṭvāṅga staff. Puṣpā, Dhūpā, Dīpā, and Gandhā are white, smoky, flame-colored, and red respectively; they have four arms and one face. In their primary single arm, they hold a flower, an incense burner, a lamp-stand, and a perfume conch; in their other three arms, they hold a hand-drum (ḍamaru), a skull-cup, and a khaṭvāṅga staff.

The mirror, tastes, touches, and phenomena are white, red, green, and yellow respectively; they have four arms and one face. With their primary right hand, they hold a mirror, a vessel of tastes, a universal vajra, and the source of phenomena (dharmodaya); in their other three hands, they hold a ḍamaru drum, a skull-cup, and a khaṭvāṅga staff.

Thereafter, having praised [the Buddhas] with the eight-line mantras to be recited, and having performed the sevenfold unsurpassed worship—consisting of the confession of sins, rejoicing in merit, the aspiration for nirvāṇa, the entreaty for the long endurance of the Victors, the supplication to the Buddhas to turn the wheel of Dharma, and the dedication of one's own merit—one should, preceded by taking refuge in the Three Jewels, relying upon the path of the Victors, offering up one’s own person, and generating the mind of awakening (bodhicitta), regard all sentient beings as if they were an only son.

In the same way, having cultivated loving-kindness (*maitrī*) characterized by the desire for union with the single flavor of great bliss; compassion (*karuṇā*) in the form of the wish to extract [beings] from suffering; sympathetic joy (*muditā*), whose nature is the desire for non-separation from the enjoyments, sovereignty, and so forth, arising from roots of virtue; and equanimity (*upekṣā*), whose characteristic is proceeding spontaneously within the true nature (*dharmatā*) that is everywhere free from aversion and attachment—one who has thus accumulated the equipment of merit (*puṇyasaṃbhāra*) should, for the sake of increasing the equipment of gnosis (*jñānasaṃbhāra*), recite: *oṃ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ*.
One should recite this preceded by bringing to mind the meaning: "All phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature.
Here, "all phenomena are pure by nature" refers to the purity of the object (*grāhya*), and "I am pure by nature" refers to the purity of the subject (*grāhaka*).
Just as a magician withdraws his magical creation once it has been produced, [so too does one withdraw the visualization].
Nothing whatsoever exists therein; for that is indeed the true nature of phenomena.

Thus, according to the scriptural teaching (*pravacana*), one should cause the three realms and the invoked maṇḍala-circle, whose nature is mere appearance, to enter into the clear light (*prabhāsvara*) alone; then, having dissolved oneself into the sun, that into the syllable *vaṃ*, that into the half-moon, that into the bindu, and that into the *nāda*, one should utter even that conceptualization by recollecting its meaning: "I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāva*)," and then let it go.

The knowledge of emptiness (*śūnyatājñāna*) itself is the "vajra" because of its indivisibility; the meaning is: "I am of the nature of that, having that as my essence. Then, by the force of the impetus of previous vows, having emerged from the meditative absorption on emptiness, one's own mind alone [appears] above and above as a bow, a triangle, a circle, and a square—transformed from the syllables *yaṃ*, *raṃ*, *vaṃ*, and *laṃ*—having the colors blue, red, white, and yellow respectively, marked with two tips shaped like moving banners, possessing flames, and having four corners marked with bells.

Having contemplated the nature of the mandalas of wind, fire, water, and earth, one should meditate upon Mount Sumeru arising above them from the essence of the syllable *suṃ*. It is square, has eight peaks, and its eastern, southern, western, and northern sides consist of silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, and gold. Then, [one recites]: *oṃ sumbha niḥsumbha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | oṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa huṃ hūṃ phaṭ | oṃ gṛhṇāpaya 2 huṃ hūṃ phaṭ | oṃ ānaya ho bhagavan vidyārāja huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.

Having thus dispelled [the obstructors] by snapping the thumb and forefinger of the left hand while reciting these four mantras, one should establish four vajra-walls—black, green, red, and yellow in color, with massive bodies of blazing fire pervading the universe from the Brahma-world to the subterranean realm (rasātala), extending as far as desired in the east, north, west, and south through the rays of the Sumbha-mantra and others—by reciting: *Oṃ vajraprākāra hūṃ vaṃ hūṃ*.

At that very moment, having recited "Oṃ medinī vajrībhava vajrabandha hūṃ," with a double-vajra (viśvavajra) empowered by the syllable *hūṃ*, one should empower the ground as consisting of double-vajras, extending down to the bottom of the netherworld (*rasātala*).

Then, having uttered "Oṃ vajraśara-jvala traṃ saṃ traṃ," one should visualize an extremely dense net of arrows above in the form of a five-pronged vajra; below that, having uttered "Hūṃ vaṃ hūṃ," the vajra-fence (*vajrapañjara*); having uttered "Oṃ vajravitāna hūṃ khaṃ hūṃ," the vajra-canopy (*vajravitāna*) in its proper place; and having said "Oṃ vajrajvālānalārka hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ," one should contemplate the vajra-flame.

Thereafter, one should visualize the four goddesses, Kākāsyā and the others, who are produced from the four mantras beginning with *sumbha*, and likewise the four goddesses, Yamadāḍhī and the others, who are born from the light rays of both sets of mantras.

These [deities] have two arms and one face; from the navel downwards they are shaped like spikes. They hold a vajra-mallet in the right hand and a kila in the form of their own body in the left. Having gone forth by means of emanation and summoned the hosts of obstructors situated in the ten directions, they enter the pits located in the cardinal and intermediate directions outside the vajra-fence—which has been produced by the long-sounding utterance of the syllable *huṃ*—and [recite]: *oṃ gha gha ghāṭaya ghāṭaya sarvaduṣṭān phaṭ phaṭ kīlaya kīlaya sarvapāpān phaṭ phaṭ*.

"*hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ vajraṃ kīlaya vajradhara ājñāpayati sarvavighnān kāyavākcittavajrakīlaya kīlaya huṃ phaṭ*. Having first recited this mantra of piercing (*kīlana*), they pierce [the obstacles]. "oṃ vajramudgaravajrakīlam ākoṭaya huṃ phaṭ. Having first recited this mantra of striking (*ākoṭana*), they strike them. One should meditate that by means of these two—striking and piercing—the host of obstacles is made of one form with great bliss (*mahāsukha*).

Again, having dispelled the remaining obstacles, while those [obstacles] dissolve into the walls, one should visualize circular walls of vajras, lotuses, and wheels for the purpose of binding the boundary, according to the principle of the emergence of droplets from the splashing of water upon water.

Having resolved that the world itself has become free of obstacles and unified into a single expanse through the purification of the expulsion of impediments such as the vajra-fence, one should contemplate within the center of a vajra-pavilion a *dharmodayā*—the nature of the *dharmadhātu*—in the form of the syllable *E*, broad at the top and narrow at the bottom. In its center, upon a universal lotus and a universal vajra, one should visualize a peaked temple (*kūṭāgāra*) consisting of Vidyāvairocana [seated] upon a *huṃ*-born lion; for there is no difference between a Tathāgata and an ordinary person, since their true nature (*tathatā*) is of a single form.

The four foundations of mindfulness constitute its square shape; the four right efforts and the bases of psychic power, through the purification of the faculties, form its four gates; it is adorned with eight pillars through the purification of the eightfold path; and through the purification of the four meditative concentrations—Śūraṅgama, Gaganagañja, Vimalamudrā, and Siṃhavikrīḍita—it is embellished with necklaces, half-necklaces, suns, moons, banners, mirrors, and chowries. In brief, through the purification of each respective Buddha-attribute, it is endowed with those specific characteristics.

At his navel, one should perceive the eight worldly dharmas as pure: within the pericarp of an eight-petaled lotus born from a red *paṃ* syllable, there is a sun mandala through the purification that dispels the darkness of ignorance; upon this is a moon mandala, the nature of the *darśana-jñāna*, produced from the doubling of the vowels (*āli*); and a sun mandala, the nature of the *samatā-jñāna*, produced from the doubling of the consonants (*kāli*) with the letters *ḍa, ḍha, da, dha, ya* omitted. The great bliss of their union is the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, situated upon the sun within a vajra-fist born from the red syllable *vaṃ* in the center of the joined mandalas.

The wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) consists in pervading that which has the nature of the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) with rays of light emanated from it, performing the welfare of sentient beings in the form of the Bhagavatī throughout the ten directions, and then withdrawing them back again into that very same place.

Through the transformation of all this, one visualizes oneself as the Blessed Lady Vajravārāhī, whose intrinsic nature is the wisdom of the utterly pure *dharmadhātu*. By virtue of the purification of great passion (*mahārāga*), she resembles the *dāḍima* flower; by virtue of the purification of the two truths, she has two arms. With her right hand, the index finger extended upward, she is intent on threatening the wicked; through the purification of the five wisdoms merged into a single flavor, she holds a red vajra. With her left hand, she holds a dry skull-staff topped with a single-pronged vajra pointing downward and a black five-pronged vajra pointing upward.

She bears a skull-cup filled with blood—the essence of the flavor of great bliss and great compassion—along with a white khaṭvāṅga staff held in her arm that is the nature of skillful means; the staff is adorned at its base with a universal vajra, a golden vase, and a universal banner accompanied by a tiny ringing bell. She has one distorted face due to the destruction of false views, and she is terrifying with prominent fangs because of her annihilation of the four Māras. Her three eyes are red with compassion, purified through body, speech, and mind.

Through the purification of the scattering of the non-dual reality (*advaitatattva*) by means of the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*), she is *Muktakeśī*, bearing the five insignias (*pañcamudrā*) known as the discus (*cakra*), the earring (*kuṇḍala*), the necklace (*kaṇṭhikā*), the breast-ornament (*rucaka*), and the girdle (*mekhalā*).
The necklace, the breast-ornament, the earrings, the crest-jewel (*śiromaṇi*),
the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), and the ash (*bhasma*) are proclaimed as the six insignias (*mudrāṣaṭka*).

Thus say some. Others say she is "sealed by the six" by virtue of being the mistress of the mandala. She is naked, endowed with fresh youth, and her nature is the fifty letters of the alphabet (*āli-kali*). She wears a garland of freshly severed human heads strung together. With her left leg bent—indicating that the world rests upon emptiness (*śūnyatā*)—and her right leg extended five *vitastis* in the *ālīḍha* posture, she tramples upon the sun-maṇḍala situated on a red eight-petalled lotus; upon this she stands, having cast down Bhairava and Kālarātri, whose natures represent the dualistic conceptualizations of eternalism and nihilism.

She possesses a solar orb of light due to her union with the radiance of perfectly pure gnosis; she is of great splendor because, being of the nature of emptiness, she is equal to the non-apprehension of the world; she flows [with blood] due to her connection with passion (*rajas*); she is fond of blood because of her constant engagement in drinking the blood dripping from the skull-cup held in her hand; she has three tufts of hair bound together by a garland of skulls—which consists of the five Tathāgatas situated between two rows of vajras; she has a crown surmounted by a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) because she is the benefactor of all beings; and she is the one who encompasses all world-systems.

One should meditate on the eight consciousnesses—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, the storehouse-consciousness (*ālaya*), and the afflicted mental consciousness—as being situated in the midst of the eight charnel grounds, by virtue of their nature as selflessness and lack of intrinsic reality.

As for the fact that in Lūyīpāda’s *Abhisamaya*, the meditation on emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is taught immediately after the *Rakṣāvajrapañjara* and so forth, that is because it is intended for those of superior wisdom; for such a person, emptiness alone is the supreme protection. However, here, for the sake of gathering all people, the protective cage and so forth are taught after the meditation on emptiness; moreover, this very sequence is seen in many *abhisamayas*. On the four petals in the east and other directions, there are, in counter-clockwise order, Dākinī, Lāmā, Khaṇḍarohā, and Rūpiṇī respectively.

They should be visualized as being black, dark blue, red, and white, each with one face and four arms; holding a *khaṭvāṅga* and a skull-cup in the left hands, and bearing a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*) and a flaying knife (*kartī*) in the right hands; they have three eyes, mouths terrifying with bared fangs, loose hair, and are naked; they stand in the *ālīḍha* posture, wear the five mudrās, and possess garlands of severed heads; they have a vajra-garland on their foreheads and a girdle at their waists, and are adorned with tinkling ornaments such as bells. In the petals of the intermediate directions, starting from the southeast and proceeding clockwise, [they are visualized] with the seminal essence (*bodhicitta*), with menstrual blood (*rajas*), with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and with the five lamps (*pañcapradīpa*).
p. 133—beginning with *mṛtībhūtaiḥ*: One should visualize four lotus vessels completely filled with [substances] that have become immortal, like the elixir of immortality (*siddharasa*).

Outside of that is the first mind-wheel (*cittacakra*), an eight-spoked wheel encircled by a garland of blue vajras. On its eastern, northern, western, and southern spokes—which possess the nature of the *pīṭhas* of Pullīramalaya, Jālandhara, Oḍiyāna, and Arbuda—are Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍākṣī, Prabhāvatī, and Mahānāsā. On the southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast—which consist of the *upapīṭhas* of Godāvarī, Rāmeśvara, Devīkoṭṭa, and Mālava—are Vīramatī, Kharvarī, Laṅkeśvarī, and Drumacchāyā.

In the second speech-wheel (*vākcakra*), which is red and surrounded by a row of red lotuses and has eight spokes, Airāvatī and Mahābhairavā reside on the eastern and northern spokes, representing the *kṣetra* sites of Kāmarūpa and Oḍra; Vāyuvegā and Surābhakṣī reside on the western and southern spokes, representing the *upakṣetra* sites of Triśakuni and Kośala; Śyāmādevī and Subhadrā reside on the southeast and southwest spokes, representing the *chandoha* sites of Kaliṅga and Lampāka; and Hayakarṇā and Khagānanā reside on the northwest and northeast spokes, representing the *upachandoha* sites of Kāñcī and Himālaya.

In the third body-wheel (*kāyacakra*), which is white and surrounded by a circle of white spokes, *Cakravegā* and *Khaṇḍarohā* reside on the eastern and northern spokes, respectively, at the *melāpaka* sites of Pretapurī and Gṛhadevatā. On the western and southern spokes, at the *melāpaka* sites of Saurāṣṭra and Suvarṇadvīpa, reside *Śauṇḍinī* and *Cakravarmiṇī*. At the southeast and southwest spokes, at the *śmaśāna* sites of Nagara and Sindhu and the *upaśmaśāna* sites of Maru and Kulūta, reside *Cakravartinī* and *Mahāvīryā*.

These goddesses, beginning with Pracaṇḍā, have one face and two arms; they hold a skull-cup filled with blood in their left hand and a threatening knife in their right. Furthermore, their dress, ornaments, and so forth are like those of the Ḍākinīs and others.

At the gates are Kākāsyā, Ulūkāsyā, Śvānāsyā, and Śūkarāsyā, like the Ḍākinīs and others; their faces follow their names exactly. In the corners are Yamadāḍhī, Yamadūtī, Yamadaṃṣṭriṇī, and Yamamathani; they have human faces, and the halves of their bodies on the left and right resemble the deities of the respective directions. All eight of these also sit upon corpses. Their remaining attire and so forth are exactly like those of the Ḍākinīs and others.
And all these goddesses are to be visualized as being instantaneously perfected at the very same moment as the perfection of the Bhagavatī.

[Ed. p. 134] Then, having performed the two armors (*kavaca*), one should perform the armor of protection as taught by Lūyīpāda, which consists of the visualization of the Wheel of Knowledge (*jñānacakra*). Having purified the sense bases (*āyatana*) with the syllables *Bhrūṃ Hūṃ Khaṃ Aḥ Hāṃ* and the letter *Ha*, one should protect oneself with Nairātmyā, just like her respective deities, using the mantras of the six goddesses: Vārāhī, Yāminī, Mohanī, Sañcāriṇī, Saṃtrāsinī, and Caṇḍikā. *Oṃ Vaṃ* at the navel; *Hāṃ Yāṃ* at the heart; *Hrīṃ Moṃ* at the mouth; *Heṃ Hīṃ* at the head; *Hūṃ Hūṃ* at the crest-lock (*śikhā*).

*Phaṭ phaṭ* for the weapon-mantra (*astra*) on all limbs. Alternatively, because there is no difference between the mantra and the deity, those very deities—produced within their respective mental images—should be visualized in those various locations.

Therein, Vārāhī has faces that are red, blue, and green; she holds a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and a noose in her left hands, and a goad, a Brahma-head, and a flaying knife in her right hands. Yāminī, Mohanī, Sañcāriṇī, Saṃtrāsinī, and Caṇḍikā are blue, white, yellow, green, and smoke-colored respectively; they have four arms and hold a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff with a bell in their left hands, while holding a hand-drum and a flaying knife in their right hands. All of them should be visualized as having loose hair, being naked, possessing three eyes, and standing in the ālīḍha posture.

Thereafter, one should place the syllables Oṃ, Āḥ, and Hūṃ—white, red, and blue respectively—upon the forehead, throat, and heart. Then, from the light rays of the seed-syllable Vaṃ, which rests upon a sun-maṇḍala situated on the center of a red eight-petalled lotus within the hub of a red vajra at the heart, one should draw in with the syllable Jaḥ the entire Wisdom Circle (jñānacakra), which consists of all the heroes and heroines manifesting in their transformed forms pervading the ten directions. Having worshipped them with offerings such as the water for the feet (argha) preceded by the sixteen goddesses, including Vīṇā and the others, who have emerged [from the seed-syllable], one should recite the syllable Phem.

Having formed the *jālāmudrā*, one should rotate it counter-clockwise on the forehead. Having caused them to enter one's own *samayacakra* like water into water by means of the syllable *hūṃ*, having bound them with the syllable *vaṃ*, and having gratified them with the syllable *hoḥ*, one should recite: "Oṃ, all phenomena are pure through yoga; I am pure through yoga. Simultaneously with the summoning of the *jñānacakra*, they are drawn forth by the Vajravilāsinīs holding skull-cups and hand-drums (*ḍamaru*) filled with the nectar of gnosis (*jñānāmṛta*), and worshipped by the goddesses such as Vīṇā who have emerged from the seed-syllable in the heart:
"Just as all the Tathāgatas were bathed immediately upon their birth..."
In that manner, I shall bathe you with pure, divine water.

Thus, having visualized oneself as the nature of great bliss being consecrated by streams of the nectar of wisdom emerging from the skull-cups held in the slightly tilted left hands of those reciting [the mantra], and having meditated on the Tathāgatas produced from the remaining water upon one's head, one should empower [the self] with: *oṃ sarvatathāgatābhiṣekataḥ samayaśriye hūṃ*.

In that regard, the Lord of the Family for the Bhagavatī is Vairocana on her head; for the Ḍākinīs and the others, it is Ratnasaṃbhava; for those situated in the wheels of mind, speech, and body, they are respectively Akṣobhya, Amitābha, and Śāśvata; and for those residing in the wheel of commitment, it is Amoghasiddhi. Thereafter, one should perform the tasting of nectar.

By means of the syllable *yaṃ*, there arises a wind mandala; above that, a fire mandala born from the syllable *raṃ*; therein, a white lotus vessel born from the white syllable *āḥ*. Upon it, resting on a crest formed by three severed heads, one visualizes the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and the five lamps (*pañcapradīpa*), presided over by the syllables *oṃ traṃ aṃ khaṃ hūṃ lāṃ māṃ pāṃ tāṃ*. Having seen these as having the color of the newly risen sun in a state of liquefaction through the seed-syllables melting under the heat of the fire ignited and fanned by the wind, one observes them extending upward for the measure of a span (*vitasti*).

Having visualized a white skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) consisting of nectar, produced from a downward-facing white *HŪṂ*, one should contemplate that even within it, due to the touch of those vapors, it dissolves; and having contemplated that which has fallen as a liquid mercury-colored, cool substance, one should again visualize the three syllables one above the other upon that. Then, by means of their rays, together with all the nectar existing within the belly of the three worlds, one should draw forth the wisdom-nectar residing in the hearts of all the Tathāgatas and dissolve it right there. Furthermore, when the three syllables have also gradually dissolved...

Having empowered oneself with the three-syllable mantra, one should meditate on a white *vajra*—the size of a *jaya* fruit—marked by a white *hūṃ*, upon the tongues of the goddesses of the mandala. Then, one should perform the consumption [of the nectar] through the tubes of its light rays. Thereafter, one should praise [them] with the eight-line worship mantras to be described below. If one is unable to stabilize the mind for a long time upon such a vast mandala-circle, then [one should focus] on the line of light rays arising from the lotus-stalk of the seed-syllable *vaṃ* situated within the union of the sun and moon at the navel-lotus.

By means of stabilizing the mind, through the cessation of the flow in the two channels of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, [the breath] enters the central channel (*madhyamā*). When the *caṇḍālī* has ignited and melted [the lunar drop], by the process of pervading the lunar wheel (*śaśicakra*) at the head, there arises the innate (*sahaja*) state through the distinctions of bliss and so forth. Due to the withdrawal of all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), there is either the simultaneous non-perception of the mandala-circle, or its gradual absorption into emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

In this regard, the sequence is as follows: the world [is dissolved] into the cremation grounds; the cremation grounds into the outer wheel (*bāhyacakra*); the outer wheel into the body wheel (*kāyacakra*); the body wheel into the speech wheel (*vākcakra*); the speech wheel into the mind wheel (*cittacakra*). Within the mind wheel, those situated in the cardinal directions dissolve into the *Ḍākinī*s and others, while those situated in the intermediate directions dissolve into the *Rūpiṇī*s and others. The *Ḍākinī*s and others, in turn, dissolve into the Blessed Lady’s mouth within the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*). The lotus seat of the Blessed Lady dissolves into the sun; the sun into Bhairava; Bhairava into Kālarātri; Kālarātri into the skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*); and the skull-topped staff into the Blessed Lady.

One should dissolve the Blessed Lady into the navel-lotus; the navel-lotus into the union of the sun and moon; the union of the sun and moon into the syllable *vaṃ*; the syllable *vaṃ* into the half-moon; the half-moon into the bindu; and the bindu into the nāda. One should perceive even the nāda as having the form of a hundred-thousandth part of the tip of a hair. Furthermore, one does not perceive even that. In this way, by virtue of the Blessed Lady’s nature as the wheel of gnosis (*jñānacakra*), there is entry into the clear light (*prabhāsvara*). Thus, one should repeatedly enter and arise. Just as the wind of the breath goes to dissolution from all sides within a mirror.
In that same way, the yogin should enter the limit of reality again and again.

Through repeated entries [into the central channel], the yogin directly realizes the *yuganaddha-samādhi*, which is perfected through the non-differentiation of the two truths. When weariness arises, one should settle the mind upon the syllable *vaṃ* located in the lotus of the navel; then, at the very moment of reciting either the *hṛdaya* or *upahṛdaya* mantra as desired from among those to be mentioned below, one should expand the five wheels (*cakras*) along with the wind exiting through the sound of that seed-syllable, perform the welfare of the world, and at the time of the wind’s entry, [contract them] by means of the mantra according to the analogy of pulling in a thread from a rosary.

One should cause them to enter together into that very [mandala]. However, for those who desire to recite the mantras of the individual goddesses that will be described, at the conclusion of the recitation of each individual goddess's mantra, the emanation and reabsorption of each must be performed as before.

Alternatively, one should visualize the garland of syllables emerging from that very [seed-syllable] as before, exiting through the mouth via the path of the *avadhūtī*, returning to its own place in the lotus, and revolving there in the same manner; or one should recite either the *hṛdaya* or the *upahṛdaya*, or the *mālā-mantra* which is about to be described. Or else, beholding that very seed-syllable surrounded by the garland of mantras like a circle of lamps, one should perform the recitation—neither too fast nor too slow, and free from improper mental constructs.

Oṃ vajravairocanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. This is the heart mantra (*hṛdayamantra*) of the Blessed Lady. Oṃ vajravairocanīye svāhā. This also is a heart mantra. Oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye vajravarṇanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. This is the near-heart mantra (*upahṛdayamantra*). These mantras possess great power. Oṃ namo bhagavatī vajravārāhi vaṃ huṃ hūṃ phaṭ. Oṃ namaḥ āryāparājite trailokyamāte mahāvidyeśvari huṃ hūṃ phaṭ.

Oṃ, homage to her who brings fear to all beings, O Great Vajra! Huṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, homage to her who dwells on the vajra-seat, the unconquered, the unconquerable, the subduer, the one who whirls the eyes! Huṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, homage to her who withers, who rages, the fierce one of wrath! Huṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, homage to her who terrifies, who slays, who pierces, the peerless one! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, homage to her who is victory, supreme victory, the paralyzer, the immobilizer, the deluder! Huṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, homage to Vajravārāhī, the Great Mistress of Yoga, the sky-goer! Huṃ hūṃ phaṭ! This is the eight-line mantra for worship of the Blessed Lady.

And furthermore, there is the garland-mantra: *Oṃ vajravārāhi protaṅge protaṅge hana hana prāṇān kiṃkini khiṃkhini ghuna ghuna vajrahaste śoṣaya śoṣaya vajrakhaṭvāṅgakapāladhāriṇi mahāpiśitamāṃsāśini mānuṣāntraprāvṛte sānnidhye naraśiromālāgranthitadhāriṇi* [ed. p. ...].

138. *Dhāriṇī*: O Sumbha-Nisumbha! Kill, kill the life-breaths! [Destroy] all the evil of sentient beings and all sacrificial animals! O cutter of great flesh! O you who are the embodiment of wrath! O you who are terrifying with fangs! O Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*)! O chief queen of the glorious god Heruka! O thousand-headed one! O thousand-armed one! O hundred-thousand-faced one! O you of blazing splendor! O flame-mouthed one! O tawny-eyed one! O you whose body is vajra! O you whose seat is vajra! Mili mili! Timili timili! He he! Ha ha! Huṃ hūṃ! Kha kha! Dhu dhu! Ru ru! Dhuru dhuru!

Muru muru! O Great Yoginī of Non-duality, perfected through recitation! *Draiṃ dhaṃ draiṃ dhaṃ graṃ*! He he ha ha! O Terrible One! Laugh, laugh! O Heroine! Hā hā ho ho huṃ hūṃ! O Destroyer of the Three Worlds! O You who are surrounded by hundreds of thousands of millions of Tathāgatas! Huṃ hūṃ phaṭ! O You in the form of a lion! Khaḥ! O You in the form of a jackal! Gaḥ! O You who transcend the three worlds! O You whose girdle is the great ocean! Devour, devour! Huṃ hūṃ phaṭ! O Non-dual Heroine! Huṃ hūṃ hā hā! O Bewilderer of the Great Beasts! O Mistress of Yoga! You, the Ḍākinī, are the one to be venerated by all the worlds.
Immediately producing conviction: *huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*, O terrifier of spirits, O great hero, O supreme adept, O mistress of yoga, *phaṭ huṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.

This mantra possesses great power and is accomplished through recitation alone. During a lunar eclipse, while beholding the moon, one should recite it until the moon is released. Thereafter, as long as one continues to revolve [the mantra], one will be followed by thousands of women. Preceded by meditative visualization (*bhāvanā*), by a single utterance one attracts, kills, and performs the rites of eradication, inciting enmity, and paralyzing those with cruel minds. If one takes charcoal from a cremation ground, recites the mantra over it once, and casts it into a house, a village, or a city, it causes a conflagration to appear.
One should whirl a peacock feather in the air, and then it becomes pacified; such are its many kinds of powers described elsewhere.

Oṃ ḍākinīye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ, for Ḍākinī; oṃ lāme huṃ hūṃ phaṭ, for Lāmā; oṃ khaṇḍarohe huṃ hūṃ phaṭ, for Khaṇḍarohā. This mantra is effective for all rites. Oṃ rūpiṇīye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ, for Rūpiṇī. Now follow the mantras of Pracaṇḍā and the others: oṃ pracaṇḍe huṃ hūṃ phaṭ; oṃ caṇḍākṣīye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ; oṃ prabhāvatīye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ; oṃ mahānāse huṃ hūṃ phaṭ.

Oṃ vīramatīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ kharvarīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ laṅkeśvarīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ dramacchāye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ airāvatīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ mahābhairavīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ vāyuvege hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ surābhakṣīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ śyāmādevīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ subhadre hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ hayakarṇe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ |

Oṃ khagānane hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ cakravege hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ khaṇḍarohe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ śauṇḍinīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ cakravarmaṇīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ suvīre hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ mahābale hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ cakravartinīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ mahāvīrye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ kākāsye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ ulūkāsye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ śvānāsye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ |

Oṃ śūkarāsye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ yamaḍāḍhīye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ yamadūtīye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ yamadaṃṣṭriṇīye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ yamamathanīye huṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Thus, first, according to the *Lūyīpāda-abhisamaya-krama*.

The mandala circle of the Goddess Bhagavatī, consisting of thirty-seven deities in detail, is written here as it was demonstrated by our own gurus in the *Vajrāvalī* immediately following the section on the types of mandalas. All the principal goddesses and others have two arms; the four Ḍākinīs have four arms. Kākāsyā and the others hold a skull-cup in the left hand and a khaṭvāṅga staff resting against their arm, while in the right they hold a ḍamaru drum. Everything else is as before.

Alternatively, the Blessed Lady is yellow or blue in color, while the four [consorts], Ḍākinī and the others, are yellow. They hold a *ḍamaru* drum in their right hands. The yoginīs of the mind-wheel (*cittacakra*) are white, with their left hands holding a vajra and a threatening gesture (*tarjanī*). Those of the speech-wheel (*vākcakra*) are black, with their right hands holding a lotus and a threatening gesture. Those of the body-wheel (*kāyacakra*) are red, holding a wheel and a threatening gesture in their right hands.

Kākāsyā and the others hold a *ḍamaru* drum in their right hands and a human skull with the index finger raised in their left hands. For Ḍākinī and the others, as well as Kākāsyā and the others, there is a *khaṭvāṅga* in the left arm. These twelve dance in a semi-circle (*ardhapaṅkti*). All else is as before. To abandon the ego-identification with the deities, to attain omniscience, and for the sake of vision, it should be understood that Ḍākinī and the others have the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*) as their intrinsic nature.

Therein, the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyānusmṛtyupasthāna*), characterized by the commencement of the thorough knowledge of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), is Ḍākinī. The application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanānusmṛtyupasthāna*), characterized by the commencement of the thorough knowledge of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*), is Lāmā. Because the aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) are illusory in nature, the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmānusmṛtyupasthāna*), characterized by retention (*dhāraṇa*), is Khaṇḍarohā. The application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittānusmṛtyupasthāna*), through the purification characterized by the differentiation of the essential nature of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), is Rūpiṇī.

The *chanda-ṛddhipāda* (basis of psychic power through desire), characterized by extreme reverence for the longing to hear the Dharma, is Pracaṇḍā. The *vīrya-ṛddhipāda* (basis of psychic power through vigor), consisting of the uninterrupted practice of vigor, is Caṇḍākṣī. The *mīmāṃsā-ṛddhipāda* (basis of psychic power through investigation), which is ultimate discernment, is Prabhāvatī. The *citta-ṛddhipāda* (basis of psychic power through concentration), which is the excellence of the intention to realize awakening, is Mahānāsā. The faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), which consists of firm conviction in the truths, the Three Jewels, and the fruits of karma, as well as mastery in the ascertainment of reality, is Vīramatī.

The faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*), which is the determination that [the practice] must necessarily be performed, is Kharvarī. The faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), which has as its sovereign power the non-forgetfulness that is the antidote to ignorance, is Laṅkeśvarī. The faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*), due to the mastery over the one-pointedness of mind, is Drumacchāyā. The faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), due to the mastery in determining what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, is Airāvatī. These very faculties of faith and so forth, when they have reached the ultimate limit of excellence, become the powers (*balas*). The power of faith is Mahābhairavā; the power of energy is Vāyuvegā; the power of mindfulness is Surābhakṣī; the power of concentration is Śyāmādevī; and the power of wisdom is Subhadrā.

Concentration alone is the cause of perfect awakening; Hayakarṇā is the factor of awakening that is concentration. The absence of opportunity for laziness is the factor of awakening that is vigor; Khagānanā is the factor of awakening that is joy, which is enthusiasm for wholesome qualities. Adaptability toward wholesome action is the factor of awakening that is pliancy; Khaṇḍarohā is the factor of awakening that is the investigation of phenomena, which is the ascertainment of the nature of selflessness; Śauṇḍinī is [that same factor].

The nature of non-forgetfulness is the mindfulness factor of enlightenment (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga), Cakravarmiṇī. Non-attention toward meditative absorption is the equanimity factor of enlightenment (upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga), Suvīrā. The practice of the non-perverted meaning is right view (samyagdṛṣṭi), Mahābalā. The non-abandonment of what has been undertaken with earnest respect is right intention (samyaksaṃkalpa), Cakravartinī. Speech that does not deceive sentient beings is right speech (samyagvāc), Mahāvīryā. Action that does not transgress the ten wholesome paths is right action (samyakkarmānta), Kākāsyā.

Right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*) is Ulūkāsyā, whose way of life does not harm sentient beings. Right effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*) is Śvānāsyā, who accomplishes the goal of virtue. Right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) is Sūkarāsyā, who recollects the words of the Buddha. Right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) is the Blessed Lady Vajravārāhī. The production of unarisen wholesome dharmas is Yamadāḍhī. The preservation of arisen wholesome dharmas is Yamadūtī. The abandonment of arisen unwholesome dharmas is Yamadaṃṣṭriṇī.
The right abandonment (*samyakprahāṇa*) is the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states (*akuśala-dharma*), and it is called Yamamathanī.

Through the purification of the ten stages (*bhūmi*)—namely, Pramuditā, Vimalā, Prabhākarī, Arciṣmatī, Abhimukhī, Sudurjayā, Dūraṅgamā, Acalā, Sādhumatī, and Dharmameghā—the internal yogin should gradually meditate upon the body-maṇḍala in the form of the *pīṭhas*, *upapīṭhas*, and so forth. As it has been said:
"The *pīṭhas* and other sites are established here according to twenty-four divisions."
Therefore, those who seek the ultimate truth should certainly not feel weary of wandering therein.
"The afflictions of those external yogins are destroyed through [this] wandering;
therefore, having rejected the external, one should abide in the system of the Yoginīs. Thus it is said.

[ed. p. 142] Therein: *puṃ*, *jāṃ*, *oṃ*, *aṃ*, *goṃ*, *rāṃ*, *deṃ*, *māṃ*, *kāṃ*, *oṃ*, *triṃ*, *kauṃ*, *kaṃ*, *laṃ*, *kāṃ*, *hiṃ*, *preṃ*, *gṛṃ*, *sauṃ*, *suṃ*, *naṃ*, *siṃ*, *maṃ*, *kuṃ*. Pracaṇḍā is at the crown of Pullīramalaya; Caṇḍākṣī is at the crest of Jālandhara; Prabhāvatī is at the right ear of Oḍiyāna; Mahānāsā is at the back of the head of Arbuda. These are the *pīṭhas*. Vīramatī is at the left ear of Godāvarī; Karvarī is between the eyebrows of Rāmeśvara; Laṅkeśvarī is at the two eyes of Devīkoṭa.

The shade of a tree over the two shoulders of Mālava is an *upapīṭha*. It belongs to the *cittacakra* and is associated with the *khecarī* [mudrā]. By means of this, there is the gathering of those who have gone to heaven.

In Kāmarūpa and Kakṣa is Airāvatī; in Oḍra, at the pair of the body [the breasts], is Mahābhairavā—this is a *kṣetra*. In Triśakuni and Nīpā is Vāyuvegā; in Kauśala and Sāgra is Surābhakṣī—this is an *upakṣetra*. At Kaliṅga-mukha is Śyāmādevī; at Lampāka-kaṇṭha is Subhadrā—this is a *chandoha*. At Kāñcī-hṛdaya is Hayakarṇā; at Himālaya-meḍhra is Khagānā—this is an *upacchandoha*. At the wheel of speech (*vākcakra*) is Bhūcarī; by her, there is the gathering of mortals.

At Pretapurī-liṅga is Cakravegā; at Gṛhadevatā-guda is Khaṇḍarohā. This is the *melāpaka*. At Saurāṣṭra, on the two thighs, is Śauṇḍinī; at Suvarṇadvīpa, on the shanks, is Cakravarmiṇī. This is the *upamelāpaka*. At Naga, on the fingers, is Suvīrā; at Sindhu, on the backs of the feet, is Mahābalā. This is the *śmaśāna*. At Maru, on the two big toes, is Cakravartinī; at Kulatā, on the two knees, is Mahāvīryā. This is the *upaśmaśāna*. At Kāyacakre is Pātālavāsinī; by her, those residing in the netherworld (*pātāla*) are included.

In this regard, the instruction is as follows: one should examine all the nasalized sounds (*anusvāra*) beginning with *puṃ*, *jāṃ*, and so forth. The sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and other locations, which are encompassed by the syllables beginning with *puṃ* and take the form of the wheel of the void of rays (*ara-śūnyatā-cakra*), are to be visualized instantaneously in the head and other parts of the body. Within those sacred seats and locations, the channels (*nāḍī*) situated in their respective places are to be contemplated as being established in the transformed form of the various deities. Just as rivers situated near external trees and such are nourished by water... [end of fragment]

Just as [the roots] perform that function, so too do the channels (*nāḍīs*) within the body nourish the nails and other parts; thus there is a similarity. Externally, the place called Mahābodhi is the Vajrapīṭha, and the river is the Nairañjanā. Within the body, the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*) is the Vajrapīṭha, and the *avadhūtī* is the Nirañjanā. At the mouth, the left and right nostrils, and the gates of the anus, Kākāsyā and the others are the female gatekeepers (*dvārapālīs*) in sequence. At the right and left ears and the right and left eyes, Yamadāḍhī and the others reside.
The four [deities], Ḍākinī and the others, are located at the heart, forehead, throat, and navel lotuses. Thus, one should repeatedly and firmly resolve upon the complete body-maṇḍala.

Then one should offer the *bali*. Having placed food and other offerings before oneself and purified them according to the previously mentioned sequence, one should visualize the maṇḍala circle—brought forth by the *jālāmudrā* and its respective measure (*tanmātrā*) and perfected in all its aspects—standing before one. After worshipping it with the *argha* and other offerings, one should see the syllable *HŪṂ* situated between the two hands, which have the nature of the moon and sun maṇḍalas transformed from the *āli* and *kāli*. Then, one recites: *Oṃ, all phenomena are mutually interpenetrating; spread forth, spread forth! All phenomena have entered [into one another], having entered utterly.*

Having first uttered "HŪṂ" for all phenomena, one should meditate on that vessel of nectar placed upon the palms of hands joined in the vajra-añjali gesture, through the transformation of the syllable HŪṂ mounted upon the moon and sun; or, for the sake of attaining the siddhi of the nectar, one should recite:
"The goddesses are the authority, their commitment is the authority, and the words they have spoken are the supreme authority.
By this truth, may these goddesses become the cause of my grace."

Then, perceiving the non-duality of the worshipper, the worshipped, the worship, and so forth, one should rotate that vessel of nectar counter-clockwise through the cardinal directions starting from the east, and clockwise through the intermediate directions starting from the southeast. While rotating it while reciting once the respective mantras of the deities of the three wheels—beginning with the Mistress whose tongue is a white vajra born of *hūṃ*—one should recite: *oṃ aralli hoḥ jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ vajraḍākinyas samayas tvaṃ*.

Saying "dṛśya ho," one should present [the offering] while reciting this once, twice, thrice, four times, or five times. Then, having given water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*), water for sprinkling the hands (*hastaprokṣaṇa*), betel, and so forth, and having worshipped with lutes and other instruments and offered praise, one should pray:

"Those whose attachment is equal to the peace of existence (*bhavaśama*), who have shattered the structure of their conceptual constructs (*saṃkalpa*), and who perceive all states of being as the void (*kha*) from the perspective of ultimate reality (*bhāvataḥ*);"
O Goddesses, whose minds are oceans overflowing with the waters of profound compassion, bestow, bestow upon me your most intense mercy!

Then, rotating [the offering] as before for the guardians of the directions stationed in the eight cremation grounds, one recites: *oṃ kha kha khāhi khāhi! May all yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, unmādas, apasmāras, ḍākas, ḍākinīs, and so forth, accept this bali-offering! Protect the pledge! Grant me all accomplishments! Eat, drink, smell, and enjoy as you please and according to your will! For the sake of increasing my true happiness in every way, be my helpers! hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!*—thus.

One should offer [the oblation] by reciting this twice. By partaking of that nectar, the guardians of the directions and the other deities should be visualized as having bodies saturated with great bliss (*mahāsukha*). Thereafter, having offered betel and so forth collectively, one should worship with the lute and other instruments emanated from the seed-syllable in one’s own heart, praise with the eight-line mantra, and pray for the attainment of desired siddhis. Then, having stirred [the offering] with the *cho-mo* hand, one should recite the hundred-syllable mantra while ringing the bell in order to fulfill any deficiencies in the ritual procedure.

Then, reciting "Oṃ, all phenomena are pure through yoga; I am pure through yoga," and having satisfied [the deities] with the *kamalāvarta* mudrā, one should dismiss them while reciting "Oṃ vajra muḥ" preceded by the withdrawal of the mudrā, the gesture of embracing, and the snapping of the left ring finger and thumb. One should cause the maṇḍala to enter into oneself in every aspect. Then, having made an aspiration, one should dwell in the form of the deity.

At the time of bathing, one should perform the ritual of consecration (*abhiṣeka*); but at the time of eating, having instantly visualized one’s own body as the nature of the maṇḍala-circle, and having offered the *bali* according to the rules, one should empower the *bali* with the three syllables, Oṃ Kha... [ed. p.]

Having offered [the food] to the guardians of the directions by reciting once the mantra beginning with *kha khāhi khāhi*, and having purified it through the ritual of kindling and so forth, one should—preceded by the pride of the equality of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanātāsamatā*)—consecrate the food and other offerings according to the rules with the mantra: *oṃ samayaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ samayaśuddho ’ham*. Then, with the pride of the equality of all phenomena, one should form a tongue consisting of white vajras produced from the syllable *hūṃ*. Having empowered it with *oṃ amṛtodaka hūṃ hūṃ ṭha ṭha trāṃ āḥ khaṃ hūṃ*, one should satisfy the syllable *vaṃ* located at the navel by means of the three syllables.

At the midday *sandhyā*, having entered the meditation chamber, one should recite these three mantras: "Oṃ āḥ hūṃ oṃ; I am of the nature of the body, speech, and mind of all yoginīs, which are by nature ageless; Oṃ, all phenomena are vajra-pure, I am vajra-pure. Reciting them, one should instantly visualize (*adhimucya*) the maṇḍala circle, perform everything as before, and dwell at ease.

At the twilight of midnight, having performed everything as at the midday twilight, and having realized that all vocal activity consists of the vowels and consonants—from *a* to *kṣa*, and uttering *huṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*—one should bring the clear light (*prabhāsvara*) before one's eyes and lie down while resolving upon the state of clear light during sleep. At the conclusion of all twilights, one should recite the hundred-syllable mantra.
Furthermore, at the morning twilight, having resolved upon the maṇḍala circle arisen from the clear light, one should perform all the previously mentioned practices.

The external ritual of worship is now described. Here, a mantra practitioner desiring to worship the Blessed Lady, having risen at dawn or at an appropriate time, and being endowed with the yoga of Vajravairocanī, should place his hand upon a clean spot and recite the mantra beginning with *oṃ sumbha ni sumbha*. Having smeared a square maṇḍala with pills made of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), fragrant substances, and so forth, or with pills of cow dung mixed with any one of those substances, he should place his hand in the center of it and [recite] the twenty-four syllables beginning with *pūjā*, as well as the ten names beginning with the seats (*pīṭha*) and sub-seats (*upapīṭha*).

And one should recite [the mantra], preceded by the resolve (*adhimokṣa*) for each respective stage. Then, in that mandala, having suddenly visualized a red lotus situated upon Mount Sumeru, which rests on the four great elements, and upon it a sun disk marked with the syllable *vaṃ*; and having brought the wisdom-mandala (*jñānamaṇḍala*) there by means of its rays and caused it to enter, one should behold the Blessed Lady together with her retinue, arisen from the transformation of that [syllable], perfected in all her aspects.

Then, having worshipped with the goddesses such as Vīṇā who have emerged from the seed-syllable in one’s own heart, and having presented the seven jewels and other offerings that have issued forth from it, one should offer the merit to the Blessed Lady in the center of the mandala using the three-syllabled mantra with the left hand purified according to the ritual rule. Furthermore, one should present [offerings] right there with the Heart-mantra and the Upahr̥daya-mantra of the Blessed Lady.

Then, one should offer merit in the maṇḍala at their respective locations for the Ḍākinīs and the others, ending with Yamamathanī, using their individual mantras—counter-clockwise in the cardinal directions and clockwise in the intermediate directions. Then, according to the sequence of hand-worship to be described, one should offer flowers with their respective mantras, beginning with *oṃ ha*, to the deities placed upon the hands at their corresponding positions.

Then, having cast the flower held in the left hand into the mandala while reciting the eight-step mantra, and having first placed his hands together in añjali at his head, he should cause the wheel of deities held in the palms of his hands to enter into himself.

Thereafter, having first offered praise with the eight-line mantra beginning with the *hṛdaya* and other hymns recited as they were practiced, and having performed the confession of sins (*pāpadeśanā*) and so forth, as well as meditation, mantra-recitation (*japa*), and the making of aspirations (*praṇidhāna*) according to one's capacity; then, having uttered the hundred-syllable mantra and satisfied [the deities] with the *kamalāvarta-mudrā* accompanied by the mantra "Oṃ, all phenomena are pure through yoga, I am pure through yoga," and then, withdrawing the mudrā while performing the gesture of embracing and snapping the fingers while reciting "Oṃ vajra mur," one should perform the dismissal (*visarjana*).
One should cause that wheel to enter into oneself; then it should be understood that one should erase the lines on the mandala.

The procedure for the hand-worship (*hastapūjā*) is now described. Therein, in the Gaṇamaṇḍala and other such rites, a yogi endowed with the yoga of Śrī Vajravārāhī should place the syllable *haṃ*—representing Vajrasattva, Vairocana, Amitābha, Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, and Amoghasiddhi—respectively white, yellow, red, black, and green in color, upon the tips of the nails of the fingers of the left hand, which are respectively the index, middle, ring, and little fingers of a Buddha. He should assign them in order with the mantras: *oṃ ha namaḥ*, *hi svāhā*, *hu vauṣaṭ*, *he huṃ hūṃ hoḥ phaṭ*.

Having meditated on a five-petaled lotus of reddish hue suddenly manifested upon the palm of the hand, one should visualize the seed-syllables *haṃ yoṃ hriṃ moṃ hreṃ hiṃ huṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ* in due order, moving counter-clockwise from the eastern petal to the others, as having the forms of Yāminī, Mohinī, Sañcāraṇī, Saṃtrāsanī, and Caṇḍikā, and possessing the colors blue, white, yellow, green, smoke-colored, and grey respectively. (Ed. p. 147, beginning with *dhūmra*).

In the pericarp, one should clearly visualize the seed-syllable *oṃ vaṃ*—which is red in color and has the nature of Vajravārāhī—or its reflection as the three wheels (*tricakra*), even upon the back of the hand below.

Then, one should visualize the elements of earth, water, fire, air, and space held in the hands as having the nature of Pātanī, Māraṇī, Ākarṣaṇī, Narteśvarī, and Padmajālinī. Then, having smeared the seed-syllables held in those hands with the liquid substance, one should visualize that palm as being the form of the three wheels presided over by all the Yoginīs. One should offer the liquid and other substances with either the three-syllable mantra or the eight-word mantra.

Then, having performed the worship and recited the hundred-syllable mantra (*śatākṣara*) for the purpose of fulfilling any deficiencies or excesses in the ritual procedure, and having requested the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the wheel and other [mandala deities], one should place that liquid in another vessel or elsewhere. Then, using the substance held in the hand—grasped by the left ring finger—one should anoint the heart, tongue, and head while uttering *HŪṂ ĀḤ OṂ*, and one should visualize that the host of deities has entered into oneself. This procedure is well known in the *Saṃcāra-tantra*. [Thus ends] the ritual for the worship of the hand.

Alternatively, reciting the ten names of the *pīṭhas*, *upapīṭhas*, and so forth, with the ring finger of the left hand purified by the previously mentioned procedure, one should draw two triangular wheels joined together using *madana* fruit purified according to the ritual rules. In their center, one should draw a circular maṇḍala. Therein, having visualized the Blessed Lady—along with her support and the supported wheel—emerging from the seed-syllable of one’s own heart and drawn by its rays, one should offer her the food, drink, and so forth, prepared in the form of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and other substances, using either the three-syllable mantra or the eight-line mantra.

Having taken the *madana* (intoxicant), which has become like nectar (*amṛta*) and is placed in a lotus vessel, with the ring finger and the thumb, one should satisfy the Blessed Lady with her own heart-mantra and sub-heart-mantra, and likewise satisfy those beginning with Ḍākinī and ending with Yamamathanī with their respective mantras. Then, having performed the worship, one should recite the hundred-syllable mantra for the purpose of fulfilling any deficiencies or excesses in the ritual procedure, and for the sake of the empowerment of the *gaṇacakra*. [End of page]

Having requested [the deities to depart], and reciting "Oṃ! All phenomena are pure through yoga; I am pure through yoga," one should satisfy them with the *kamalāvṛtana* mudrā. Then, withdrawing that mudrā while performing the gesture of embracing and touching the ground with the ring finger, one should recite "Oṃ vajra mur," dismiss them, and cause that maṇḍala-circle to enter into oneself.

Then, having taken the *madana* (betel nut) that has been placed on the ground with the left ring finger, one should smear the heart, tongue, and head with it while preceded by the utterance of the syllables *HŪṂ ĀḤ OṂ*. One should visualize that the wheel of deities residing in that [nut] has also entered into oneself; thus is the worship performed with the hand described. Then, with the mantra *OṂ ŚUKLA OṂ*, one should offer the other oblation with the right *sruva*-ladle—[the ladle being] a vajra-tongue transformed from the syllable *OṂ*—into the mandalas filled with garlands of flames situated upon the pericarp of the lotus at one’s own navel. This concludes the remainder of the internal fire offering (*adhyātmahoma*).

Oṃ āḥ ucchiṣṭavajra, empower this bali offering, hūṃ svāhā! Within the non-dual fire of wisdom in the form of the wheel of the three realms, which consists of emptiness and compassion, the unsurpassed homa consists of burning the aggregates and so forth according to the oral instructions. As for the external homas for pacification, enrichment, and so forth, they should be performed following the rules for the fire-pit, flowers, sacrificial wood, drying, and other requirements as prescribed in the *Homa-vidhi* according to the specific rite. The detailed procedures have not been written here for fear of prolixity.
Thus, the visualization of the Blessed Lady together with the mandala has been explained in detail, including the rites of worship and the offering of the bali.

One should meditate on the fivefold mandala as follows: for those with moderate inclination, there are the four Ḍākinīs and so forth in the cardinal petals, the samaya-substances placed in lotus-vessels in the intermediate petals, and the Blessed Lady as described in the center. The offering of bali, worship, and so forth, should be performed for these five with their respective mantras as appropriate. The protection circle and other rites are exactly as before. Furthermore, according to the sequence emerging from Oḍiyāna, she stands with her feet upward; the seed-syllable of accomplishment and the heart-mantras and others are the same, and the Ḍākinīs and so forth are likewise.

One who seeks a concise meaning, however, meditates solely upon the Blessed Lady in the form already described. The worship and other rites should be performed for the Blessed Lady as previously instructed. In some cases, she is visualized as follows: having worshipped the Buddhas and others brought forth by the rays of light from the white syllable *oṃ* situated on the moon at one’s own heart, and having contemplated emptiness, she is manifested seated upon a lotus and moon, arisen from the seed-syllable *vaṃ* within a moon and vajra.

Furthermore, this very Bhagavatī Vajravairocanī is called Vajrayoginī; and regarding her, there are many varieties of oral traditions (āmnāya) according to the scriptures and according to the instructions.

It is as follows: having visualized upon the triangular fire-maṇḍala arising from one’s own navel a red circular lotus with a red syllable *hrīṃ*, and through the total transformation of that [syllable], one should meditate on oneself as the Blessed Lady Kolāsyā, who is red in color, stands in the *ālīḍha* posture treading upon a corpse, has tawny hair on her head, and possesses four arms. With her two right hands she holds a vajra and a goad; with her two left hands she holds a khaṭvāṅga and a skull-cup, as well as a noose with a raised index finger. She has a large belly and a boar’s face. Her remaining form is as before. This is the sequence of Śrī Vajraghoṇā.

The specific [mantras], however, are as follows: *oṃ hūṃ hrīṃ traṃ* is the heart [mantra]. *oṃ vajravārāhī āveśaya sarvaduṣṭān hrīṃ svāhā* is the near-heart [mantra]. Through recitation of these characteristics preceded by the yoga of the Goddess, success is attained; of this there is no doubt. With this mantra, *oṃ āḥ hrīṃ hūṃ haḥ haḥ*, one should offer incense made from powdered human flesh (*mahāmāṃsa*). Before the cloth painting (*paṭa*), within twenty-one days, the desired goal is accomplished.

One should utter *oṃ hrīṃ haṃ hāṃ haḥ haḥ hiḥ hīṃ hīṃ hīṃ pheṃ pheṃ* as the sound of the offering. For the purpose of pacifying all Māras, the *niśāvali* (night-offering) should be presented with the fivefold service (*pañcopacāra*). This ritual procedure must not be disclosed to those who are uninitiated; by it, the Vajrayoginīs bestow their blessing. *Oṃ hrīṃ ghātaya sarvaduṣṭān hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Having first offered the *bali* with this mantra, one should perform this *sādhana* of Vajraghoṇā.
Although the ritual for the *bali* and so forth have been mentioned previously, they are performed here as well; indeed, what is more extensive is to be praised.

In some cases, she arises from the transformation of a red five-pronged vajra, which is presided over by a white syllable *hrīḥ* situated upon a sun disc produced from the syllable *āṃ* within a heart-lotus of blood; she stands in the *ālīḍha* posture atop a sevenfold ignorance-man (*puruṣa*) on a sun disc resting upon a white and red lotus; her heart-vajra rests upon a sun disc presided over by a red syllable *hrīṃ* situated on a sun disc; and she is born from the consecration of Akṣobhya, who rests upon a sun disc on a universal lotus (*viśvapadma*). All else is as before.

Thereafter, having visualized the syllable *hrīḥ* upon a red and white solar disc situated on a universal lotus at the navel, one should imagine that garland of its mantra-mantras in the form of a white rosary issues forth from the opening of the mouth by means of the "wheel-rotation" (*cakrabhramaṇa*) yoga. Taking up the power of the multitude of Buddha-qualities, jewels, mantras, medicinal herbs, the moon and stars, scripts, treatises, arts, and so forth, one should meditate on it as entering through the opening of the navel, consisting of the burning away of all ignorance in oneself and others. One should recite the mantra, free from defects such as being too fast or slow. The mantra is: *hrīṃ hrīṃ*.

When one wishes to rise, then, having internalized the mantra-garland within the syllable *hrīṃ* located at the navel and performed the worship and other rites, one should dwell at ease. Furthermore, having visualized a red *hrīṃ* syllable of blazing and radiant form upon one's own tongue—which has the appearance of a lotus petal born from the syllable *āḥ*—and having fixed the mind there, one should recite [the mantra] with a rosary of fifty beads during the four or three junctions of the day.

Thus, a yogi endowed with the practice of recitation and meditation becomes, through seven hundred thousand recitations, an expert in all scriptures and arts, intelligent, a quick learner, one who cannot be overcome by any assembly, a debater, and a great poet. He cannot be withered or afflicted by fevers, spiders, *ḍākinīs*, and the like. When this mantra has been mastered, if a pen consecrated with this mantra is placed in someone's hand, even if that person is a fool, he becomes a poet.

For the purpose of subjugation (*vaśya*), however, one should visualize her as red in color and, having performed the ritual according to rule by tasting nectar, one should see the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*)—produced from the syllables of one's own name—drawn in by rays of light emerging from the mantra-garland and brought before oneself. Then, observing the mind in the form of a red moon-disc transformed from the syllable *oṃ*, one should behold the goddess, red in color, emerging from that mantra-garland, holding a noose marked with the syllable *hrīḥ* in her left hand and a vajra-hook resembling the bud of a red lotus in her right, standing before the person to be acted upon.

Then, immediately after issuing the command: *Oṃ āḥ hrīḥ, draw forth the mind of [Name], hūṃ jaḥ*, that goddess enters the body of the subject according to the ritual procedure; she encircles the moon-maṇḍala of the mind with her noose, impels it with her hook, draws it into her own mind, and becomes absorbed within the mantra-garland. Thereafter, one should meditate upon that subject—with palms joined, solitary, utterly dependent, facing the practitioner—saying, "What shall I do?"

Thus, by meditating at the four junctions of the day or the three junctions, one will certainly bring the object of accomplishment under control before long. Furthermore, in some traditions, she is visualized as follows: she is the transformation of a red *hūṃ* syllable situated upon a moon on a universal lotus; she stands in the *ālīḍha* and *pratyālīḍha* postures treading upon corpses; her red hair blazes upward; she has two arms, with her right hand brandishing a severed [skull-topped staff] and making the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*), and her left hand holding a skull-cup filled with blood; all other ornaments and attributes are as described previously. Oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye oṃ vajravarṇanīye oṃ vajravairocanīye hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā. This is the root mantra.

Oṃ vajraḍākinīye hrūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | This is the heart mantra (*hṛdayamantra*). Oṃ vajrayoginīye hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | This is the near-heart mantra (*upahṛdayamantra*). Oṃ vajraḍākinīye imaṃ baliṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa ha ha ha ha ha kha kha kha kha a a a a mama siddhiṃ prayaccha hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | With this mantra, having consecrated [the offering] with nectar as before, the *bali* should be given. Specifically, it should be offered at night on the eighth day and other such occasions in a cremation ground.

In some instances, she is seen born from a red *hūṃ* syllable with her mass of hair loose; in others, she is without a corpse. The mental recitations (*adhimantra*), however, remain the same. In another case, she is born from a yellow *hrīḥ* syllable in the center of a vermilion-red *dharmodayā*, which rests upon a sun disk on a white lotus at her own navel. She herself holds her own severed head in her left hand, while her right hand holds a flaying knife (*kartī*). Her left arm is extended upward, her right arm is bent downward, her right leg is stretched out, and her left foot is drawn up.

A stream of blood, having issued from the severed neck of Kabandha, falls into his mouth; others, having issued from the tongues of the two female attendants, enter the mouths of the two Yoginīs at his sides—thus it should be visualized. On the left side is Śyāmavarṇā Vajravarṇanī, holding a flaying knife in her left hand and a skull-cup in her right, with her left leg extended.

On the right side is Vajravairocanī, yellow in color, holding a flaying knife (*kartī*) in her right hand and a skull-cup (*kapāla*) in her left; her right leg is extended and her left leg is drawn up. The rest is as before. *Oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye oṃ vajravarṇanīye oṃ vajravairocanīye hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*. This is the mantra for recitation (*jāpamantra*).

The worship is described as follows: having drawn the *dharmodayā* above the sun situated within a square maṇḍala, and having visualized the syllable *hrīṃ* in its center, one should perform the worship. Therein, in the center of the *dharmodayā*, one should first worship with the mantra beginning "Oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye" and so forth. One should offer the water for the feet (*argha*) and other offerings with this: "Oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye hūṃ svāhā. On the left, one should worship with "Oṃ vajravarṇanīye hūṃ svāhā," and on the right with "Oṃ vajravairocanīye hūṃ svāhā."

Then, having formed the names of Oḍiyāna, Pūrṇagiri, Kāmarūpa, Śrīhaṭṭa, Dharmakāya, Saṃbhogakāya, Nirmāṇakāya, and Mahāsukhakāya, each ending in the dative case, and having worshipped them with the mantra beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *svāhā*, one should dismiss them as before. However, in another ritual procedure, one should resolve that this palace is the purification of one's own body and the three realms. Instantly, at the center of the navel, one should meditate on the goddess who has two faces, holds a curved knife and a skull-cup in her hands, sits in the half-lotus posture, performs the *tāṇḍava* dance, and resembles a hibiscus flower in color. Her right face is that of a boar, and her left face is likewise that of a wrathful deity.
"But by means of the purification of the two truths, the two faces are proclaimed.

Thus, having taken this up, one should understand that there are infinite traditions (āmnāyas) of the Blessed Lady, which have come down through a lineage of perfected masters' instructions and vary according to the different dispositions of those to be trained. Only a mere indication has been shown here. And among these sequences, one who possesses faith and so forth, taking up a single sequence, being free from attachment, observing the pledges, and meditating without doubt, will certainly achieve accomplishment.

The preliminary worship as it has come down in the oral instructions is written here: On the tenth day, having prepared saffron and other substances in a clean vessel, one should drop vermilion into it. In the center of that, having drawn a *dharmodayā* with a golden stylus, one should write the syllable *hrīṃ* in its center. Then, having drawn the *nandyāvarta* mudrā on the sides, one should worship it with water and flowers. One should worship the four seats (*pīṭha*) beginning with Oḍiyāna and the four bodies (*kāya*) as before.

One should offer whatever foodstuffs, drinks, and other substances for the ritual commitment (*samayadravya*) are available. One should also worship a young maiden (*kumārī*). This rite must be performed in strict secrecy by one who is naked, with hair disheveled, and seated facing south. Otherwise, there will be a loss of accomplishment (*siddhi*) and various kinds of diseases will arise. Then, having offered the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) and made a prayer for the desired accomplishment, one should dismiss [the deity] and give the vermilion, the food offering, and so forth, to young maidens or to women whose husbands are living.

Furthermore, on the tenth, eighth, or fourteenth day, whatever flowers, fruits, oil, betel, rice, vegetables, leaves, curd, wood, salt, vermilion, fish, or meat may be sold by women such as Māmakī and others—having purchased some small amount of any such thing according to one's means and prepared it appropriately, one should, as before, write the seed-syllables and so forth within a *dharmodaya* fashioned from vermilion, worship it, pray for the attainment of one's desired goal, and then perform the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*).

From this point forward, as before, it is taught that one receives consolation from the Vajra-women in dreams. Furthermore, on the eighth lunar day, having applied vermilion (*sindūra*) upon the surface of a perfectly polished mirror, one should draw the *dharmodaya* mudrā thereon; having inscribed the seed-syllable *vaṃ* in the outer corners and the mantra in the center, and having drawn a *nandyāvarta* in a counter-clockwise direction on the four sides outside the *dharmodaya*, one should worship it with flowers and other offerings, recite the mantra as much as possible, and [collect] that "vermilion of recitation" (*japasindūra*).

One should place it in a single vessel. One should do this for six months. Then, having placed that vermilion (*sindūra*) inside a hollow reed (*viṣanalikā*) dedicated to Lāṅgalī, one should bury it in a cremation ground. Having performed the offering (*bali*) and worship, one should recite the mantra as desired. One should perform this daily for one month. Having fashioned a *nandyāvarta*-shaped tilaka with that vermilion, one should enter the village for alms.

One should diligently propitiate that woman in whom that *tilaka* is seen to have been transferred. Thus is the procedure for the propitiation of Vajrayoginī according to the tradition of the Siddha Śabarapāda by means of the *nandyāvarta*.

In this Yoginī-naya, one who abides in it should perform worship, mantra-recitation, eating, and so forth, secretly with the left hand. For those undertaking a pilgrimage to sacred sites (*pīṭha*) and the like, circumambulation of villages, cities, and so on should be performed counter-clockwise (*vāmāvarta*) for the sake of the Vajra-ḍākinīs. When walking, one should proceed by first extending the left foot forward. Whatever the five objects of desire (*pañcakāma*) may happen to be encountered, they should be enjoyed without hesitation as the purification of Vairocana and the other [Buddhas].

One must not perform rites of sorcery against those who are well-behaved or innocent. Women must not be beaten, nor should they be provoked to anger, nor should they be held in contempt—especially those who bear the six mudrās. Having understood these various types of commitments (*samaya*) according to the tantras, they must be observed. Mantras and other such elements should also be employed after being learned from that very source; they are not written here for fear of prolixity. In short: the Guru is the Buddha, the Guru is the Dharma, and likewise the Guru is the Saṅgha;
the Guru is the glorious Vajradhara—the Guru alone is the cause in this matter.
"Therefore, one desiring the fruit of Buddhahood should propitiate the Guru. Having established this,

Therefore, one should strive to attain this fresh and exceedingly beautiful cluster of blossoms, which arises from the wish-fulfilling tree of clear realization.
